questions.question: REINFORCE updates vary sharply because episode returns are noisy. What state-dependent quantity can be subtracted without changing the expected policy gradient?
options: The transition probability for every possible next state.
A baseline b(s) that does not depend on the selected action.
The maximum reward observed in a separate environment.
A different action probability chosen after observing the return.
questions.explanation: For any baseline b(s) independent of the sampled action, its expected score-gradient contribution is b(s)∇Σaπ(a|s)=b(s)∇1=0, so the expected policy gradient is unchanged. A well-fitted value baseline can reduce variance; an action-dependent correction would not cancel this way.

questions.question: In actor-critic, which pairing correctly describes the actor and critic roles?
options: The actor selects terminal states; the critic enumerates the model.
The actor stores transitions; the critic chooses the reward function.
The actor estimates state value; the critic samples policy actions.
The actor samples policy actions; the critic estimates state value.
questions.explanation: The actor is πθ(a|s), the policy that samples actions; the critic is Vφ(s), the expected-return estimate trained by regression. Swapping them assigns policy selection to the value model and value prediction to the policy.

questions.question: Which advantage target is the Monte Carlo form, with lower bias but higher variance than the one-step TD form?
options: r_{t+1} plus gamma V_phi(s_{t+1}) minus V_phi(s_t).
The current value estimate minus the next action probability.
G_t minus V_phi(s_t), using the full return from time t.
The maximum action value minus the mean reward over the batch.
questions.explanation: The Monte Carlo advantage subtracts the critic from the full return, A=Gt−Vφ(st), so it avoids bootstrapping bias but retains full-return variance. The one-step TD option uses r+γVφ(s′)−Vφ(s), which bootstraps and trades some bias for lower variance.

questions.question: For generalized advantage estimation, what do lambda = 0 and lambda = 1 represent?
options: Both values produce the same n-step estimate.
Lambda 0 removes the critic; lambda 1 removes the actor.
Lambda 0 is Monte Carlo; lambda 1 is one-step TD.
Lambda 0 is one-step TD; lambda 1 is Monte Carlo.
questions.explanation: GAE weights TD residuals by (γλ)^l. At λ=0 only the current one-step residual remains; for a completed episode, λ=1 sums the residual sequence to the Monte Carlo return. The reversed-endpoints option swaps the low-variance TD and higher-variance MC cases.

questions.question: A team wants synchronous batched updates across many GPU environments, with one update per combined rollout. Which architecture fits the lesson?
options: A3C, which pushes worker gradients asynchronously to a shared server.
REINFORCE, which requires a different policy for every worker.
Independent Q-learning, which updates separate tables without a batch.
A2C, which gathers parallel environments and updates synchronously.
questions.explanation: A2C gathers rollout steps from N parallel environments into a combined batch, then applies a synchronous update. A3C instead has workers push gradients asynchronously, so that design does not match the requested GPU-batched update.

questions.question: An A2C trainer wants to reuse each rollout for many gradient epochs. What method change addresses the on-policy data constraint described in the lesson?
options: Remove the critic and keep reusing the same actor samples.
Switch to A3C because asynchronous gradients make old data on-policy.
Keep A2C unchanged because its gradient remains on-policy indefinitely.
Use PPO's clipped importance ratio to support multiple rollout epochs.
questions.explanation: A2C’s data is on-policy, so after its single update the actor has changed and the old rollout no longer matches the current policy. PPO’s clipped importance ratio corrects for that policy change during multiple epochs; asynchronous workers alone do not make stale data on-policy.
